catalog_locator: Forku 2000: sec. 0.7 'Typology', p.9; ch.1 'Tones', p.15; sec. 4.1, p.60; General Conclusion, p.95. Ndedje 2003: sec. 1.3 'Les tons', p.26.
catalog_quote: [p.9, 0.7 Typology] The Màmə́nyán language is a tone language. Without this tone, it will be impossible to get the meaning of a word since we found many words in the language which differ only in their tones. Examples 1: [mə̂ŋgúp] 'hen' [mə̂ŋgùp] 'shoes' [pé] 'payment' [pè] 'profit' ... [p.15, Chapter 1 Tones] As a tone language, Màmə́nyán has the pitch phenomenon of tone which functions in the language as a feature associated with vowels and syllabic nasals. When analysing this language, we found words whose meaning differed just because of their tones. ... 1.1 Inventory of tones. Two types of tones are found in the Màmə́nyán language: level tones and contour tones. ... [p.60, 4.1] In Màmə́nyán, the nucleus is defined by a tone which is born either by a vowel or a syllabic nasal N. ... [p.95, General Conclusion] After the examination of tones, four tonemes were attested: the H tone, the L tone, the HL tone and the LH tone. ... [Ndedje 2003 p.26, 1.3 Les tons] L'inventaire des tons a permis de dégager deux types: Les tons ponctuels (H/B) et les tons modulés (BH/HB). Ceci permet en filigrane de relever que mə̀ŋgambo est une langue à tons comme beaucoup d'autres langues africaines. Ces tons, lorsqu'ils sont associés aux voyelles et aux nasales syllabiques, ont une fonction distinctive. ... les quatre (4) tons lexicaux identifiés dans cette langue sont tous des tonèmes.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: The language is described purely as a tone language with four lexical tonemes (H, L, HL falling, LH rising) carried by vowels and syllabic nasals; the description makes no statement of any kind about word stress or accent (neither a position nor a denial). Ndedje 2003 (p.26) independently says the same: 'mə̀ŋgambo est une langue à tons', four tonemes H, B, BH, HB, again with no stress statement.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the conclusion (p.95-96) lists upstep, downstep and downdrift as tonal phenomena left for future study.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on citation-form words (1,300-item corpus); no word- or phrase-level stress/accent domain is discussed in either thesis.
new_statements.identity_note: Both theses describe the speech of Bamenyam village (25 km from Mbouda, Bamboutos Division, West Region, Cameroon), ALCAM code 908, Ethnologue/ISO bce = Glottolog bame1260. Forku 2000 calls it Màmə́nyán (autonym); Ndedje 2003 calls it mə̀ŋgambo/Mengambo (another name for the same village language, per his sec. on ALCAM 908 and Ethnologue BCE). No dialect split is described.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the same work the existing catalog statement is drawn from; re-reading it confirms the quoted sentences verbatim on the rendered page scan (pp. 20, 26, 106) and confirms that nothing about word stress appears anywhere in the thesis. The catalog record has an empty rule; 'tone language, no stress statement' remains the correct entry.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lexical tone language with four tonemes (H, L, HL, LH) carried by vowels and syllabic nasals; the thesis (a full phonology sketch: tones, vowels, consonants, syllable structure, orthography) contains no section or sentence on stress, accent or prominence. The only hits for 'stress'/'accent' in the whole text are the idiom 'I would like to stress the fact' (acknowledgements) and a quoted Dubois et al. 1973 definition of the toneme as an 'accentuated high unit'.
new_statements.identity_note: Forku 2000 sec. 0.6 (p.6): 'Maŋga'ma, identified by Michel, Dieu et al (ALCAM 1983:122) as Màmə́nyán is assigned code 908.. This language has no dialect.' Ndedje 2003 ch.0 (p.9): code 908 = mamənyán (ALCAM 1983), 'mə̀ŋgambo' per Breton & Fohtung (ALCAM 1991), Ethnologue code BCE 'Bamenyam' (Grimes 1992); natives prefer 'maŋga'ma'. So Màmə́nyán, Mengambo/mə̀ŋgambo and Bamenyam [bce] are one language, spoken in one village; no dialect variety is described by either work.

new_statements.quote: [p.26] L'inventaire des tons a permis de dégager deux types : Les tons ponctuels (H/B) et les tons modulés (BH/HB). Ceci permet en filigrane de relever que mə̀ŋgambo est une langue à tons comme beaucoup d'autres langues africaines. Ces tons, lorsqu'ils sont associés aux voyelles et aux nasales syllabiques, ont une fonction distinctive. [...] L'étude des tons permet d'inférer que les quatre (4) tons lexicaux identifiés dans cette langue sont tous des tonèmes. [p.67] Le mə̀ŋgombo utilise deux hauteurs mélodiques : H (´) et B (`). Ces tons peuvent s'associer pour donner des tons modulés du type HB (^) et BH (ˇ).
new_statements.translation: [p.26] The inventory of tones brought out two types: level tones (H/L) and contour tones (LH/HL). This shows in passing that mə̀ŋgambo is a tone language like many other African languages. These tones, when associated with vowels and syllabic nasals, have a distinctive function. [...] The study of tones allows us to infer that the four (4) lexical tones identified in this language are all tonemes. [p.67] Mə̀ŋgombo uses two melodic pitch levels: H (´) and L (`). These tones can combine to give contour tones of the type HL (^) and LH (ˇ).

new_statements.relation_note: Independent second source (author studied the same village, Bamenyam, with his own informants; ch.0 gives ALCAM 908 / Ethnologue BCE / native name maŋga'ma for the same language) confirming that Màmə́nyán is a four-toneme tone language and adding nothing on stress; agrees with the existing Forku 2000 statement and the 'tone language, no stress statement' reading.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nominal-morphology thesis whose phonology chapter (ch.1, largely summarising Forku 2000) states that the language is a tone language with two level tonemes (H, B) and two contour tonemes (BH, HB), distinctive on vowels and syllabic nasals; ch.2 gives the tonal structure of noun radicals. No statement on stress, accent or prominence anywhere (text-layer hits for 'accent' are only the idiom 'mettons l'accent sur', p.~70; 'hauteur' refers to vowel height and tone pitch).
